\[
S(m,n)=\frac{m+1}{n}+\frac{n+1}{m}\qquad (m ,n\in \Bbb Z_{>0}).
\]

We shall show that there are infinitely many couples \((m,n)\) with \(S(m,n)\in \Bbb Z\).
It is enough to exhibit infinitely many solutions for a single integral value of
\(S(m,n)\); we choose the value \(4\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Reducing the problem to a Diophantine equation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Putting \(S(m,n)=4\) and multiplying by \(mn\) gives  

\[
m(m+1)+n(n+1)=4mn\Longrightarrow
 m^{2}+n^{2}+m+n-4mn=0. \tag{1}
\]

Regard (1) as a quadratic in \(m\):

\[
m^{2}+(1-4n)m+(n^{2}+n)=0.  \tag{2}
\]

For (2) to possess an integral root \(m\) its discriminant must be a perfect
square:

\[
\Delta=(1-4n)^{2}-4(n^{2}+n)=12n^{2}-12n+1=t^{2}  \tag{3}
\]

for some integer \(t>0\).
Equation (3) is still quadratic; we transform it into a classical Pell type
equation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A Pell equation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put  

\[
y=2n-1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad n=\frac{y+1}{2}\quad (y\ {\rm odd}>0).
\]

Substituting \(n=(y+1)/2\) in (3):

\[
t^{2}=12\Bigl(\frac{y+1}{2}\Bigr)^{2}-12\Bigl(\frac{y+1}{2}\Bigr)+1
      =3y^{2}-2. 
\]

Hence we must solve  

\[
t^{2}-3y^{2}=-2. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Infinitely many solutions of \(x^{2}-3y^{2}=-2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Equation (4) is a Pell equation with parameter \(d=3\) and right–hand side
\(-2\).  It has the small positive solution \((t_{0},y_{0})=(1,1)\) because
\(1^{2}-3\cdot1^{2}=-2\).

Let \((a,b)=(2,1)\) be the fundamental solution of
\(x^{2}-3y^{2}=1\) (since \(2^{2}-3\cdot1^{2}=1\)).
Because the norm (the left–hand side) is multiplicative,

\[
(t+y\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)^k,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,
\]

Writing  

\[
(t_{k}+y_{k}\sqrt3)=(1+\sqrt3)(2+\sqrt3)^k\qquad(k\ge 0) \tag{5}
\]

Explicitly (multiplying out (5))

\[
t_{k+1}=2t_{k}+3y_{k},\qquad
y_{k+1}=t_{k}+2y_{k},\qquad (t_{0},y_{0})=(1,1). \tag{6}
\]

every \(y_{k}\,(k\ge 0)\) is odd and positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\[

\]

\(t_{k}^{2}\), hence (2) has two integer roots

\[

\]

\[
4n_{k}-1=2y_{k}+1>t_{k}\quad
(\text{because }(2y_{k}+1)^{2}-t_{k}^{2}
 =(y_{k}+1)(y_{k}+3)>0),
\]

positive integers.

symmetric solution \((n_{k},m_{k})\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------------------

(1), hence

\[
\frac{m_{k}+1}{n_{k}}+\frac{n_{k}+1}{m_{k}}=4\in\Bbb Z.
\]

\((m_{k},n_{k})\) – grow strictly, the pairs \((m_{k},n_{k})\)

\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

{"kind":"proof","text":"Let G and H be nonabelian groups of order 21. By Sylow’s theorems, the number of Sylow 7-subgroups divides 3 and is congruent to 1 modulo 7, so each group has a unique, hence normal, Sylow 7-subgroup. Write P=⟨b⟩ in G and R=⟨d⟩ in H, where b and d have order 7. Choose elements a∈G and c∈H of order 3.

Since ⟨a⟩∩P={e} and |⟨a⟩||P|=21, every element of G has a unique form b^s a^r, with s modulo 7 and r modulo 3. Similarly, every element of H has a unique form d^s c^r.

Because P is normal, conjugation by a induces an automorphism of P, so

a b a^{-1}=b^i

for some i∈{1,2,3,4,5,6}. Since a^3=e, conjugating three times gives b=b^{i^3}, hence i^3≡1 (mod 7). The solutions are i∈{1,2,4}. If i=1, then a and b commute; as they generate G, this would make G abelian. Thus i∈{2,4}. Likewise,

c d c^{-1}=d^j

for some j∈{2,4}.

Choose x∈H as follows: if i=j, let x=c; if i≠j, let x=c^{-1}. Since 2 and 4 are inverses modulo 7, in either case x has order 3 and

x d x^{-1}=d^i.

Also ⟨x⟩=⟨c⟩, so every element of H has a unique form d^s x^r. Define

φ:G→H, φ(b^s a^r)=d^s x^r.

This is well-defined and bijective by uniqueness of the two normal forms. Moreover, from a^r b^t a^{-r}=b^{i^r t},

(b^s a^r)(b^t a^u)=b^{s+i^r t}a^{r+u},

where exponents are reduced modulo 7 and 3. The identical formula holds in H because x^r d^t x^{-r}=d^{i^r t}. Therefore

φ((b^s a^r)(b^t a^u))=φ(b^s a^r)φ(b^t a^u),

so φ is a bijective homomorphism. Hence G≅H. Therefore any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.","reason":"The proof uses Sylow theory to obtain unique normal forms, identifies the only two possible nontrivial conjugation actions, and constructs an explicit isomorphism after replacing one order-3 generator by its inverse when necessary."}

By Sylow's theorems, the number \(n_7\) of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups satisfies \(n_7\mid 3\) and \(n_7\equiv1\pmod 7\), so \(n_7=1\). Thus \(G\) has a normal cyclic subgroup \(N=\langle b\rangle\) of order \(7\). Let \(H=\langle a\rangle\) be a Sylow \(3\)-subgroup. Since \(N\cap H=\{e\}\) and \(|N||H|=21\), we have \(G=NH\).

Normality of \(N\) gives
\[
aba^{-1}=b^r
\]
for some \(r\in\{1,\ldots,6\}\). Because \(a^3=e\), conjugating three times gives \(b=b^{r^3}\), hence \(r^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(r\equiv1,2,4\pmod 7\). If \(r=1\), then \(a\) and \(b\) commute, and because they generate \(G\), the group would be abelian. Thus \(r=2\) or \(r=4\). If \(r=4\), replace \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\); the induced automorphism is then the inverse of exponentiation by \(4\), namely exponentiation by \(2\) modulo \(7\). \[
a^3=b^7=e,\qquad aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]

Applying the same argument to \(G'\), choose generators \(c,d\) such that
\[
c^3=d^7=e,\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^2.
\]

Define
\[
\Phi:G\to G',\qquad \Phi(b^j a^i)=d^j c^i.

This is well-defined and bijective by uniqueness of the normal forms. Moreover,
\[

\[
